message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe.

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Common isotope** | ^1H (protium) – 99.98 % natural abundance |
| **Other stable isotopes** | ^2H (deuterium, 0.02 %) and ^3H (tritium, radioactive, ~10⁻¹⁰ %) |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average weighted by natural isotopic composition) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Second ionization energy** | 24.587 eV (2375 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative, meaning it releases energy when gaining an electron) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0000899 kg m⁻³) |
| **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas |
| **Bonding behavior** | Forms covalent bonds; diatomic molecules (H₂) dominate under normal conditions. Can form hydrides with metals (metallic hydrogen), ionic compounds (hydrohalides, e.g., HCl), and acids (e.g., H₂SO₄). |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; reacts with oxygen to form water (combustion). Combines with many elements to form hydrides. |
| **Uses** | Fuel (fuel cells, rocket propellant), hydrogenation reactions, ammonia synthesis (Haber process), metal processing, semiconductor manufacturing, medical imaging (MRI contrast agents using deuterated compounds). |
| **Physical characteristics** | Colorless, odorless, tasteless gas; very light; forms a weakly polar molecule (dipole moment ≈ 0.112 D). |

**Key points**

* Hydrogen is the lightest element and exists naturally as a diatomic gas (H₂).
* It has three stable isotopes; deuterium and tritium are used in nuclear fusion research and tracer studies.
* Its low boiling/melting points mean it remains gaseous until cooled below about –260 °C.
* Despite being a simple atom, hydrogen plays a central role in chemistry, biology (as part of water and organic molecules), and astrophysics (stellar nucleosynthesis).
